IV12-01.solved: NIMBLE = quick and light in movement; 'agile' is the standard one-word equivalent. 'graceful' names beauty of movement, not quickness; 'sturdy'/'upright' are build and posture.
IV12-01.note: All four options are common adjectives of comparable length and register. 'graceful' is the right kind of near-miss for an opener.

IV12-02.solved: BOAST = speak with excessive pride about oneself; 'brag' is the exact synonym.
IV12-02.note: 'announce' shares only the speech-act genus; 'complain' and 'insist' are not close. Fine as an opening item but the distractors do not come from any wrong path a student would actually take.

IV12-03.solved: FORBID = prohibit; 'outlaw' is prohibit by rule. 'enforce' is the opposite side of a rule, 'review' and 'delay' are procedural.
IV12-03.note: All four are transitive verbs of comparable frequency. 'enforce' is a good trap (same semantic field, opposite role).

IV12-04.solved: SPARSE = thinly dispersed, few and far between = 'thinly scattered'. 'crowded together' is the antonym.
IV12-04.note: Phrase-form options, all four adverb+participle and parallel; no length or shape tell.

IV12-05.solved: BAFFLE = bewilder, confound = 'puzzle'. 'discourage' and 'irritate' are the emotional consequences sometimes attending confusion, not the sense.
IV12-05.note: All four are common transitive verbs taking a person as object; register is even.

IV12-06.solved: OBSTINATE = stubbornly refusing to change course = 'unyielding'.
IV12-06.note: Well-built set: all four are un- adjectives of similar length, so the prefix carries no information. Best-constructed synonym item in the batch.

IV12-07.solved: VIGILANT = keeping careful watch for danger = 'watchful'. 'apprehensive' is fearing danger, not watching for it.
IV12-07.note: Register flag, but in the safe direction: 'apprehensive' is markedly longer and rarer than patient/hopeful/watchful, and it is a DISTRACTOR, so the odd-word-out heuristic does not find the key. 'patient' is weak.

IV12-08.solved: LENIENT = mild and forgiving in punishment = 'merciful'.
IV12-08.note: 'hesitant' is the useful trap (both look like softness/reluctance to act). All four common adjectives, even register.

IV12-09.solved: DIMINISH = become or make smaller = 'dwindle'. 'fluctuate' is change without direction, 'stabilize' is the opposite, 'linger' is persistence.
IV12-09.note: Slight mismatch of valence only: 'dwindle' is intransitive-only while DIMINISH is both, which ISEE tolerates. 'fluctuate' is a genuinely good distractor for a student who has only 'changes in amount'.

IV12-10.solved: ARDUOUS = requiring great and sustained effort = 'demanding'. 'tedious' is tiresome length/dullness; 'hazardous' is risk. Effort, not boredom or danger.
IV12-10.note: Mild register flag: 'demanding' is the plainest and commonest of the four (hazardous/unfamiliar/tedious are all a step up), so a student guessing by feel may be pulled AWAY from the key toward the harder-looking 'tedious' - the safe direction, but the set is not register-flat. 'tedious' is the strongest distractor in the synonym half.

IV12-11.solved: SUPERFLUOUS = more than is needed, excess = 'unnecessary'.
IV12-11.note: Register flag: 'uncorroborated' is well outside ISEE Upper Level vocabulary (it is a GRE-band word) and is four syllables longer than everything else in the set. It is a distractor, not the key, so it cannot be picked off by odd-one-out, but the set is not of comparable frequency. Consider 'unexplained/unnecessary/unfinished/unproven'.

IV12-12.solved: PARSIMONIOUS = extremely sparing with money = 'unwilling to spend'. 'openhanded' is the antonym; 'unable to save' inverts the direction (stinginess is not poverty).
IV12-12.note: Phrase options all parallel and all about money, so the field cannot be narrowed without knowing the word - which is what a hard synonym should do. 'unable to save' is the best distractor here.

IV12-13.solved: INDOLENT = habitually averse to exertion = 'lazy'. The other three are different character faults (fear, inattention, physical awkwardness).
IV12-13.note: Register is even - timid/careless/lazy/clumsy are all everyday adjectives - so no frequency tell despite the hard headword. This is the right shape for a hard item.

IV12-14.solved: CAPRICIOUS = given to sudden unaccountable changes of mood or purpose = 'inconstant'.
IV12-14.note: REGISTER FLAG, and this is the one that matters: 'inconstant' is the only literary/elevated word in the set (secretive, forgetful, exacting are ordinary). A student who has learned that hard headwords take hard answers can pick the key by register alone without knowing CAPRICIOUS. Replacing a distractor with something like 'fastidious' or 'implacable' would flatten it.

IV12-15.solved: The map shows a bridge that no longer exists and has not been reprinted since; it is therefore out of date. 'outdated' is the only option the washed-out-bridge + no-new-printing pair supports.
IV12-15.note: All four options are adjectives that sit grammatically in the blank and all four are negative descriptions of a map, so polarity carries no signal. Good easy opener.

IV12-16.solved: Read twice before opening, parts laid out in diagram order, finished quickly - planned and orderly = 'methodical'. 'improvised' is the opposite of reading ahead; 'fortunate' and 'inspired' deny the preparation the sentence describes.
IV12-16.note: All grammatical; all four are neutral-to-positive, so the key is not a polarity singleton.

IV12-17.solved: North-facing greenhouse, back bench farthest from the glass, and the stem explicitly rules out water and feed ('watered and fed on the same schedule'). The one variable left is distance from the glass = light.
IV12-17.note: All four are nouns and grammatical. 'water' and 'fertilizer' are explicitly excluded by the stem rather than merely unsupported, which makes them weak; the live contest is light vs 'space', and only light is licensed by 'farthest from the glass' and 'north wall'.

IV12-18.solved: Every ingredient is named; no quantity, temperature or time is given. The card is missing parts of what a set of directions must contain = 'incomplete'.
IV12-18.note: 'impractical' is the closest second and I considered it seriously; it describes the consequence of the gap rather than the gap, and the stem's structure (names X, gives not one Y) points at the missing content itself. I would still watch this one in item stats - it is the narrowest margin among the easy-medium completions. All four options are adjectives and grammatical.

IV12-19.solved: Four hundred at the first meeting, thirty by November - the popularity did not last = 'short-lived'.
IV12-19.note: POLARITY FLAG: 'short-lived' is the only option that undercuts, against three neutral-to-positive options (universal, deserved, deliberate). A solver who never reads the stem knows the sentence is doing a reversal from the 'but'-shaped narrative and can pick the one negative word. Swap one distractor for something equally deflating ('overstated', 'localized') to close it.

IV12-20.solved: Amendment requires the vote of EVERY living member; two members on the roll cannot be reached. Therefore no amendment can obtain the required vote - in practice the document cannot be amended.
IV12-20.note: POLARITY/INTENSITY FLAG: all four options are 'adjective + to + verb' and grammatical, but the key is the only ABSOLUTE among three gradable inconveniences (tiresome, expensive, awkward). The stem's 'whatever the clause was meant to protect' signals a strong reversal, and the only strong option is D - narrowable without the stem's specifics. Also note the key is the only option whose verb ('amend') echoes the stem's first clause; the other three verbs are all about reading/using the document.

IV12-21.solved: The label gives only name, year, medium and nothing about the scene, sitter, or provenance; to a visitor who wants to know what he is looking at, it does not help = 'unhelpful'. Nothing says it is wrong ('inaccurate') or describes its appearance.
IV12-21.note: All adjectives, all grammatical. 'inaccurate' is the useful trap - it tests the distinction between wrong and insufficient, which item 28 tests again.

IV12-22.solved: Second half explains the blanks: three names 'set down at the head of the entry' = precise about who proposed; 'the rest of it says only that there was discussion' = silent about who opposed. Both halves must fit, and only 'precise . . . silent' does; 'brief . . . thorough' inverts the informativeness.
IV12-22.note: Both members of every pair are grammatical in their blanks. The two-blank form is standard for ISEE Upper Level and the pairs are well matched. 'cautious . . . admiring' is the weakest pair (neither half is supported).

IV12-23.solved: Crossed whenever the tide allowed, never twice at the same hour, but failed only once in thirty years: perfectly reliable, wholly unpredictable in timing = 'irregular'. Nothing in the stem bears on cost, speed or space.
IV12-23.note: All four adjectives grammatical and all four are complaints, so polarity is flat - good. But three of the four are unsupported by any detail in the stem, which makes them weak: the stem's whole second clause exists only to set up 'irregular'.

IV12-24.solved: The bylaw covers lampposts and leaves the fence, the shelter and the library wall untouched; as a rule against flyposting it reaches only some of the surfaces = 'partial'.
IV12-24.note: All four adjectives sit grammatically in the blank ('its coverage is illegal' is odd semantically but not ungrammatical). 'symbolic' is the closest second but requires importing an intent the stem never gives; 'partial' is the only one the enumeration of uncovered surfaces licenses.

IV12-25.solved: Counted in February, when the summer cottages are empty and their owners counted in the cities: the figure understates August's population, so taken as an August figure it misleads.
IV12-25.note: 'generous' is an excellent distractor because it is wrong by DIRECTION - a February count is too low, not too high - so it catches a student who felt the mismatch without tracking its sign. All four grammatical; 'identical' and 'unavailable' are weak. Polarity flat enough (three of four are defects).

IV12-26.solved: Pencil, erased in place, new figure written in the same square: the current value survives and the prior value is destroyed. The books show what every figure is but not what it replaced.
IV12-26.note: The hard item of the batch and a fair one: the erasure detail is load-bearing and is the only thing that discriminates 'replaced' from the generically attractive 'means'. All four options are verbs that fit 'what it -------' grammatically, though tense is mixed across the set (means/totals present, cost/replaced past); the key is not alone in past tense, so no tell.

IV12-27.solved: Every post-1931 edition copied the coastline from its predecessor, so all of them inherit the errors of the 1931 survey; a copy is no more accurate than what it was copied from = 'source'.
IV12-27.note: All four nouns are grammatical after 'no more accurate than their'. 'scale' is the one a student might reach for from general map knowledge; the chain-of-copies structure only supports 'source'.

IV12-28.solved: By Vandermeer's OWN standard the study needed n>=400 and had 91, so the finding may still be true - the stem grants 'not so much wrong' - but nothing in the study establishes it. That is 'unsupported'.
IV12-28.second_defensible: D - 'imprecise'. A sample a quarter of the required size is also a straightforwardly imprecise estimate, and 'not so much wrong as imprecise' is an idiomatic contrast between truth and resolution. I judge 'unsupported' the better answer (the stem measures the study against a methodological THRESHOLD for validity, not against a margin of error, and 'imprecise' would normally describe the wording or the estimate rather than the evidential standing), but a competent student can reach D by a real reading, not a mistake.
IV12-28.note: The only item in the batch where I would not call the key uniquely defensible. The fix is cheap: replace 'imprecise' with something that cannot express an evidence deficit ('unpopular', 'premature' would be no better - try 'unfashionable' or 'derivative'). 'disputed' and 'exaggerated' are clean - nothing says anyone contested it, and n does not bear on the size of the claimed effect. All four grammatical.

IV12-29.solved: In four of the last six years exactly one eligible novel existed, so winning means being the only entrant; what the win records is how few competitors there were = the 'size' of the field.
IV12-29.note: 'field' collocates with size in exactly this idiom, which is a small collocational help but requires the arithmetic point to be understood. All four nouns grammatical. 'generosity' and 'ambition' are unsupported; 'age' is weak.

IV12-30.solved: A clause meant to settle the boundary forever is the very thing the parties are now fighting over, because 'at the river' no longer identifies one line. The device intended to end argument is where the argument comes from = 'origin'.
IV12-30.note: 'resolution' is the right kind of trap - it is what the clause was MEANT to be, and the stem's 'has turned out to be' demands the reversal. All four nouns grammatical after 'the ------- of the dispute'.
